title: A priest with no temple
translation: Koretsugu, a counsellor at court, had a real gift for poetry. He kept the Buddhist rules all his life and was always reciting the sutras, and for a while he was staying with Bishop En'i of Mii-dera. Monks from Mii-dera were called "temple priests", to tell them apart from the "mountain priests" of Mount Hiei.
When Mii-dera was burned down in 1319, Koretsugu went to see the bishop and said, "I used to call you a temple priest. But there's no temple now, so from now on I'll just call you a priest."
original: {惟継|これつぐ}{中納言|ちゆうなごん}は、{風月|ふうげつ}の{才|ざえ}に{富|と}める{人|ひと}なり。

{一生|いつしやう}{精進|しやうじん}にて、{読経|どきやう}うちして、{寺法師|てらほふし}の{円伊僧正|ゑんいそうじやう}と{同宿|どうしゆく}して{侍|はべ}りけるに、{文保|ぶんぽう}に{三井寺|みゐでら}やかれし{時|とき}、{坊主|ばうず}にあひて、「{御坊|ごばう}をば{寺法師|てらほふし}とこそ{申|まう}しつれど、{寺|てら}はなければ{今|いま}よりは{法師|ほふし}とこそ{申|まう}さめ。」といはれけり。
いみじき{秀句|しうく}なりけり。
literal: Middle Counsellor Koretsugu was a person rich in talent for (poetry on) wind and moon.

All his life he kept the abstinences and recited sutras, and while he was lodging together with Bishop En'i, a temple priest, when Mii-dera was burned in the Bunpō era, he met the master of the lodging and said, 'I have called Your Reverence a temple priest, but since there is no temple, from now on I shall call you a priest.'

notes.text: Taira no Koretsugu (1266–1343), a court noble with a background in Chinese learning. {中納言|ちゆうなごん}: Middle Counsellor, a senior post in the council of state.
'Talent for wind and moon': a gift for poetry, especially poetry in Chinese, whose standard subjects these were.
{精進|しやうじん}: keeping the Buddhist rules, especially avoiding meat and fish. Modern {精進料理|しやうじんれうり} is the vegetarian temple food.

Mii-dera (Onjōji) and Enryakuji on Mount Hiei were both Tendai temples, and bitter rivals. People called the monks of Mii-dera {寺法師|てらほふし}, 'temple priests', and those of Enryakuji {山法師|やまほふし}, 'mountain priests'. Their quarrels often ended in fire.

notes.quote: 文保に三井寺やかれし時
notes.text: In 1319 (the third year of Bunpō), monks from Enryakuji attacked Mii-dera and burned it. It was not the first time.
{坊主|ばうず}: the master of a priest's lodging ({坊|ばう}), here En'i. Modern ぼうず is a casual or rude word for any monk, or a little boy.

notes.quote: 寺はなければ今よりは法師とこそ申さめ
notes.text: The joke is in the word itself: take the temple away from a temple priest, and only the priest is left. こそ … め: the realis form of む, 'I shall call you'.

notes.quote: いみじき秀句なりけり
notes.text: {秀句|しうく}: a clever line, a witticism. Kenkō judges it as wordplay and says nothing more.
